title: Algebra
overview: Extend algebraic technique to harder polynomials, partial fractions with repeated or quadratic factors, and the general binomial expansion for any rational n. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Solve equations and inequalities involving |ax + b| and interpret modulus graphs.
Divide polynomials of degree at most 4 and use the factor and remainder theorems.
Decompose proper rational functions into partial fractions, including repeated linear and irreducible quadratic factors.
Expand (1 + x)ⁿ for rational n and state the interval of validity after any substitution.

definitions.definition: |x| is the non-negative distance of x from 0.
The remainder when f(x) is divided by x − a is f(a).
x − a is a factor of f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0.
A rational expression whose numerator has lower degree than its denominator.
An expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ that is infinite when n is not a non-negative integer.

sections.title: Modulus equations and inequalities
content: Treat |u| as a distance. For b > 0, |u| = b gives u = ±b, |u| < b gives −b < u < b, and |u| > b gives u < −b or u > b. For expressions on both sides, critical points or squaring can help, but every solution must satisfy the original relation.
bullets: Sketch y = |ax + b| by reflecting negative y-values above the x-axis.
Use interval notation or a number line to communicate inequality answers clearly.

examples.label: Key relationship
examples.content: Modulus interval: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b

sections.title: Polynomial division and theorems
content: Write missing powers with zero coefficients before long division. If f(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r, then r = f(a). Use known factors to reduce a cubic or quartic, then solve the remaining factor completely.
bullets: For a divisor ax + b, test x = −b/a.
Match coefficients only after expanding both sides in descending powers.

sections.title: Partial fractions
content: First check that the fraction is proper. Use A/(ax+b) + B/(cx+d) for distinct linear factors, A/(ax+b) + B/(ax+b)² for a repeated factor, and (Bx+C)/(x²+d) over an irreducible quadratic. Cover-up works for simple linear factors; substitution and coefficient comparison finish the rest.
bullets: Polynomial division comes before decomposition when degrees are equal or numerator degree is larger.
A quadratic denominator needs a linear numerator.

sections.title: General binomial expansion
content: Use (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2! + n(n−1)(n−2)x³/3! + ⋯. Rewrite expressions into this form first. The series is valid for |x| < 1, so after substituting x = g(t), solve |g(t)| < 1.
bullets: Keep exact fractional coefficients until the final line.
Only include the requested highest power; cross-terms can contribute to it.

formulas.label: Modulus interval
formulas.expression: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b

formulas.label: General binomial
formulas.note: Valid for |x| < 1 when the expansion is infinite.

examTips: State the range of x for every infinite binomial expansion.
When a factor is ax + b, use its root −b/a rather than b.
Show the mathematical setup and exact working before the final rounded answer; unsupported calculator output may not earn method marks.
commonMistakes: Decomposing an improper rational expression before polynomial division.
Putting a constant numerator above an irreducible quadratic factor.
Forgetting that a strict modulus inequality gives strict endpoints.

quickRecall.question: What partial-fraction numerator belongs above an irreducible quadratic?
quickRecall.answer: Use a linear numerator, for example (Bx + C)/(x² + d).

quickRecall.question: How do you test whether x − a is a factor?
quickRecall.answer: Calculate f(a); it is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0.

quickRecall.question: What is the validity condition for a general binomial expansion?
quickRecall.answer: The substituted quantity playing the role of x must have modulus less than 1.

quickRecall.question: Why check modulus solutions?
quickRecall.answer: Squaring or splitting cases can introduce values that do not satisfy the original equation or inequality.
